items.reviewer_notes: A medium-tier jumble engineered so that the expected shape (claim, mechanism, examples) is wrong and the actual shape (claim, examples, generalisation) is fixed by one phrase. Heuristic solvers who order by 'general before specific' lose here.

items.title: The Bus That Emptied No Cars
items.theme: what free public transport actually changes
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); the v2 exemplar
items.reviewer_notes: A concession-turn item where the last sentence does real work: it keeps the author from the conclusion the evidence seems to invite. Three distortion families: logic (the turn collapsed), stance (flipped to dismissal), addition (a prescription).

items.title: The Pill That Works Before It Dissolves
items.theme: why placebo effects are largest for pain, and what makes them larger still
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); the v2 exemplar
items.reviewer_notes: A medium-tier item where the outlier shares the noun, the field and a connective with the core. The item teaches that 'therefore' is not a passport: a sentence must serve the paragraph's purpose, not merely follow from its topic.

items.title: Following Without Believing
items.theme: why a valid proof can fail to persuade: the proof as certificate versus the proof as explanation, and reading for the one decisive step
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-01
items.reviewer_notes: A foundation short: problem, diagnosis, remedy in three signposted paragraphs. The detail question carries the near-tie (a single negation separates the finalist from the key); the purpose question offers the memorable distinction as a decoy for the passage's actual job.

items.title: Set Apart and Forbidden
items.theme: how the category of the sacred moved from the property of the gods to whatever a community sets apart and forbids, and whether extending it to godless societies was a discovery or a redefinition
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-01
items.reviewer_notes: A short history-of-an-idea in three stages, closing on an unresolved dispute. The EXCEPT question tests stage-tracking (which stage said what); the inference question lives on the defenders' single sentence; the main-idea question offers each stage's content as a thesis.

items.title: The Repair That Was a Move
items.theme: why reforms produce consequences their designers did not intend: a reform as a move that invites a reply, not a repair to a machine
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-01
items.reviewer_notes: An analogy-driven short: the repair versus the move, carried by the chess image and three one-line examples. The final paragraph qualifies the analogy (people are not opponents), and every question is designed to punish readers who take the vehicle of the analogy for the claim.

items.title: Register · the right word for the room
items.reviewer_notes: The first register bundle: twenty sentences whose genre — a notice, a contract, a methods section, a recipe, an obituary, a commentary — fixes which of four near-synonyms belongs. Wrong options carry the right meaning in the wrong room, the wrong colouring, the wrong strength, or a collocation the sentence refuses.

items.title: Register · the room's own verb
items.reviewer_notes: The stretch register bundle: the rooms are subtler — an academic hedge, a court's ruling, a communiqué, a forecast, a leaflet, an opinion column's escalation — and several options are formal but wrong in sense.

items.title: Connotation · the same meaning, a different colour
items.reviewer_notes: The first connotation bundle: each sentence carries an attitude in its other words — admiration, complaint, alarm, tenderness — and only one of four near-synonyms carries the same attitude. The traps are the approving word in a disapproving sentence and the reverse, plus the word at the wrong strength.

items.title: The Question the Pilot Never Asks
items.theme: why pilots succeed and rollouts fail: a pilot measures efficacy under attention while a rollout depends on a supervisory capacity that cannot be extended, so the two are different questions rather than one biased measurement
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-01
items.reviewer_notes: Two accounts of the pilot-to-scale gap are given their due and then both refused, not because they are false but because they answer the wrong question. The near-tie sits in the agreement question, where a distractor converts the author's 'not sufficient' into 'irrelevant'.

items.title: Worth Watching
items.theme: why satire fails against a figure who cannot be shamed: its force is borrowed from what the target has staked on an audience's good opinion, and what survives is an audience-facing function the author refuses to call equivalent
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-01
items.reviewer_notes: A narrative that looks like an anecdote about a spoiled joke and is really about where a joke's force comes from. The set punishes the two easy readings: that the sketch was at fault, and that the closing paragraph is a consolation.

items.title: What Travels and What Does Not
items.theme: food prohibitions versus food procedures as boundary markers: the first is kept alone and portable, the second requires co-performers, so dispersal dissolves a shared practice into a stated identity without anyone abandoning anything
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-01
items.reviewer_notes: A contrast passage whose two terms are easy to state and hard to keep apart under pressure. The set turns on cost: abstention is paid by one person, coordination by a group, and almost every distractor is built by forgetting which is which.

items.title: The Sentence You Cannot Finish
items.theme: whether language shapes thought: obligatory grammatical marking as a habit of attention built by repetition, replacing the picture of a grammar that walls off what its speakers can think
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-01
items.reviewer_notes: A foundation-level passage on a topic usually written badly. The familiar strong claim is stated and refused in the second paragraph, so every question is really a test of whether the reader kept the refusal. No named languages and no trivia: the illustration is hypothetical on purpose.

items.title: Good Form
items.theme: manners as moral practice rather than decoration: a manner claims nothing about feeling, which is why it can make consideration reliable, and why an arbitrary code can still be judged by whether it puts a stranger at ease
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-01
items.reviewer_notes: Two objections are conceded at length before the turn, so the passage reads for two paragraphs as an attack on its own thesis. The set is built to catch readers who stop at either concession, and the scope question checks whether the reader kept the narrowed version at the end.

items.title: Nine Times in Ten
items.theme: explaining a belief versus justifying it: why the causal question is asked only after the verdict, and the single condition under which a causal story really does bear on a belief's standing
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-01
items.reviewer_notes: A claim, then a carefully drawn exception. The whole set turns on one substitution the passage anticipates and refuses: readers who take the qualification to be about the believer's motive rather than about the process will pick the wrong option three times out of four.

items.title: Due for a Change
items.theme: the gambler's fallacy and the expectation of a streak as one habit meeting two assumptions about the source, and why only one of the pair is an invalid inference
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-01
items.reviewer_notes: The hardest item in the batch. Everything depends on which assumption about the source yields which expectation, and the two are easy to swap under time pressure; the application question is built to punish exactly that swap. The final paragraph breaks the symmetry the rest of the passage has been building, which is where the agreement question lives.

items.title: The Hour That Was Never Enough
items.theme: why our estimates of how long work will take stay wrong however often they are corrected
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A foundation-tier jumble with no engineered trap: one general claim, one case, one explanation and one closing qualification, each carrying a plain signal. It exists to teach the two habits the harder items assume — open with the sentence that needs nothing before it, and let explicit connectives place the rest.

items.title: The Empty Wall Beside the Picture
items.theme: why the bare wall a gallery leaves around a painting is part of how the painting is seen
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A foundation-tier argumentative jumble whose only difficulty is a repeated noun. 'Wall' appears in the first and last sentences of the correct order, which invites a solver to glue them; the connectives override the repetition. Written to teach that a shared word is a hypothesis, not a link.

items.title: The Numbers Nobody Would Allow
items.theme: how quantities less than nothing were used for two centuries before they were admitted to exist
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: An advanced chronological jumble built on one weaponised connective. The 'Yet' sentence shares its vocabulary with the opening sentence and looks glued to it; the relative clause inside it names a denial that only the second sentence makes, so the pair must be separated. A surface solver who follows repeated words gets this item wrong.

items.title: The Map Made of Smells
items.theme: the evidence that ocean-going seabirds find their way home partly by scent
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: An easy claim-and-evidence jumble whose tail is locked by one demonstrative. No trap is engineered, but a mild lexical decoy joins the opening claim to the sentence about open water; the demonstrative in the final sentence settles the order regardless.

items.title: The Biscuit and the Reach of Fleets
items.theme: how the keeping qualities of food and water, not doctrine, set the limits of naval power
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A ninety-nine tier five-sentence jumble whose difficulty is concentrated at the tail: three candidate endings, separated only by a 'therefore', a definite phrase and a demonstrative. The opening is also contested, since the sentence about biscuit begins with a bare noun and only a possessive pronoun betrays its dependence.

items.title: The Explanation Nobody Can Check
items.theme: whether a right to be told why an automated decision went against you is worth anything without the means to contest the answer
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A premium four-sentence jumble in which the false join is made by a repeated noun across a question and a finding, and broken by a demonstrative inside the finding. The paragraph is abstract throughout and offers no chronology or example to fall back on, so the solver must work purely from reference.

items.title: The Judgement That Could Not Be Inherited
items.theme: why an organisation built on one person's good judgement fails after that person leaves, and what can be done about it in advance
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A cat-plus problem-and-solution jumble whose trap is placed at the head rather than the tail. The decoy opener has every surface property solvers look for in a first sentence and two definite references that disqualify it; the real opener is the least quotable sentence in the set.

items.title: The Street That Keeps You Interested
items.theme: the hypothesis that a street's pleasantness depends on how often it gives the walker something to notice, rather than on its beauty
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A premium hypothesis-and-support jumble locked by a measurement rather than by a connective. The two supporting sentences are parallel cases that must run in one direction only, because the second borrows its length from the first; the closing inference is marked as an inference by a single modal.

items.title: The Quiz That Teaches
items.theme: why recalling material is a better way to learn it than reading it again, and why the effort is the point
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: An easy-tier jumble that teaches the anchor-pair defence in its mildest form. Two sentences share the vocabulary of retrieval and look inseparable; the tail is settled by one definite phrase. Written so that a solver who reads for reference rather than for repetition gets it quickly.

items.title: The Cost of Making a Deal
items.theme: why so much economic activity is organised by instruction inside firms rather than by prices in a market
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A cat-plus jumble built on definite articles. Three sentences open with the — the claim, the reason, and a demonstrative pointing at costs — and each points at a different antecedent. The decoy is a pair of sentences that share the vocabulary of markets and prices while answering different questions.

items.title: Register · four formal words, one formal room
items.reviewer_notes: The elite register bundle. Unlike the core and stretch sets, slang is almost never the answer's rival: in every item all four options are educated, formal words, and the discrimination is which professional room wrote the sentence — a judgment, a minute, a statute, a referee's report, a policy, a will. Three rivals per item fail on a locatable ground: the verb takes the wrong object, the act named is a different act, or the word imports a feeling the genre does not express.

items.title: Connotation · the colour the sentence has already chosen
items.reviewer_notes: The second connotation bundle, a band harder than the core set. Each sentence contains its own verdict — a consequence, a clause of concession, a gloss after a colon, an explicit denial — and the four options share a denotation while differing in what they think of it. The rivals are not slang: they are respectable words whose approval, disapproval, intensity or scope the sentence has already excluded.

items.title: Only One Thing at a Time
items.theme: counterfactual history as a disciplined method: every causal claim already contains a counterfactual, the discipline is a minimal rewrite and a short chain, and what a good one establishes is contingency rather than an alternative past
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-02
items.reviewer_notes: A definition-then-application passage where the two conditions stated in the second paragraph decide four of the five questions. The near-tie sits in the inference question, where a narrow vote satisfies the first condition and a reader is invited to treat that as enough to settle what the alternative would have produced.

items.title: The Second Judgement
items.theme: applying trial evidence to an individual patient: the average is an estimate for whoever resembles the enrolled, so the real judgement is about resemblance, and an unnamed difference is not a reason to depart from the result
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-02
items.reviewer_notes: The passage refuses both familiar positions, which is what the relationship and agreement questions are built on. The fourth paragraph rejects the sceptic and the fifth refuses to let the manualist collect the winnings, and readers who stop after the fourth carry away half the argument.

items.title: A Multiplier, Not a Gift
items.theme: the rule of law as a formal virtue whose worth is conditional: predictability makes usable whatever room the law's content leaves, so it multiplies liberty rather than supplying it
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-02
items.reviewer_notes: Three short paragraphs, three positions, and a thesis that arrives only in the last four sentences. The formal account stated in the opening paragraph survives into the author's view, which is what makes it the strongest wrong answer to the main-idea question.

items.title: The Tools That Happened to Fit
items.theme: why mathematics invented for its own sake so often fits the physical world: most of it never fits, physicists go looking for the parts that do, and a small residue of exact prediction survives the explanation
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-02
items.reviewer_notes: A foundation item: plain sentences, one claim, two supports and a short concession. The only real work is keeping the concession of the third paragraph out of the author's case, which is what the EXCEPT question tests.

items.title: Finding, Not Finding Out
items.theme: intent in criminal law as an imputation made from conduct by standing presumptions, which answers the objection that mental states cannot be observed but narrows the difference the traditional defence of intent relies on
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-02
items.reviewer_notes: The adjudication in the third paragraph rescues one side and then charges it for the rescue in the fourth, so options that make the author a defender of the mental element are attractive throughout. The weaken question's rival restates the author's own qualification about displacement and supplies no frequency, which is the element the key adds.

items.title: The True Thing He Said
items.theme: lying against misleading: the defence that the hearer completes the inference fails once the sentence was chosen for that inference, and what survives is a difference in what the deceiver has staked, which matters where the standing of assertion needs protecting
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-02
items.reviewer_notes: The hardest item of the batch. The passage destroys one defence of a distinction and then rebuilds a narrower one on a different footing, so every question turns on which of the two differences an option is talking about: the contribution to the false belief, which the author denies differs, or the exposure, which he says does.

items.title: Judged Against a Memory
items.theme: why cuisines change so much more slowly than dress: a dish is judged against a remembered version and sits inside a tuned system, so departure reads as error rather than novelty until circumstances remove the choosing
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-02
items.reviewer_notes: A short passage with two mechanisms and a closing pivot that turns the whole account round. The pivot is what makes sentiment the wrong answer everywhere in the set, and the word in the last clause carries two opposed senses, only one of which the sentence can take.

items.title: A Good Test in the Wrong Room
items.theme: why a highly accurate test can still be mostly wrong: accuracy belongs to the instrument while the worth of a positive result belongs to the instrument together with the population, so the same test changes value when it changes room
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-02
items.reviewer_notes: The arithmetic is given in words so that no calculation is required, and every question is decided by the third paragraph's separation of two quantities rather than by the numbers. The near-tie is in the inference question, where improving the test is offered as the remedy for a problem the test is not causing.

items.title: The Test of Saying So
items.theme: the ethics of nudging: the complaint about influence proves too much because no arrangement is neutral, so the objection should be narrowed to influence that works only while the chooser is unaware of it
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-02
items.reviewer_notes: A long passage written at foundation difficulty: short sentences, concrete examples, a signposted five-step argument. The work is in the last paragraph, which limits the test the fourth paragraph has just proposed, and which most of the harder options are built to catch readers who stopped before it.

items.title: What the Reader Knows Yet
items.theme: the order of telling as a choice rather than an ornament: order fixes what a reader knows when each event arrives, so it decides which questions are available, without any order being better than another
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-02
items.reviewer_notes: A concession-then-thesis passage where the concession is unusually firm: rearrangement is refused any credit at all, twice. That is what makes every option ranking one order above another wrong, and it is the commonest thing a reader supplies for himself.

items.title: The Prize for Guessing Highest
items.theme: why the winner of an auction for an unknown quantity is systematically the bidder who overestimated it
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A cat-tier jumble built around a single decoy opener. The sentence a heuristic solver will place first is the third sentence of the paragraph, and the only thing that refuses it is a two-word ordinal deep inside a clause. Lexical repetition also misleads: the opening advice and the closing discipline share the vocabulary of bidding.

items.title: What the Courts Did When God Stopped Answering
items.theme: how a prohibition on clerical participation in the ordeal forced English courts to improvise a lay method of deciding facts
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A cat-plus chronology whose difficulty is a shared noun. Two sentences end on the word verdict and invite a solver to weld them; a third sentence has to stand between them, and the only evidence for that is a reported absence. The date sentence is also a decoy opener.

items.title: The Engineer With Four Legs
items.theme: why returning beavers to a valley slows water as effectively as concrete flood defences
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A beginner item that teaches one move: find the owner of a pronoun. The surface signals all point the right way, so a careful reader who checks references will solve it directly; the only decoy is that engineers also build dams.

items.title: The Tune That Stopped Changing
items.theme: how writing a living practice down rescues one version of it and quietly ends the variation that produced it
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A medium item in which the only hard evidence is arithmetic. A dozen becomes one plus eleven, and the two references to eleven fix the last two sentences absolutely. The 'Yet' is a decoy: it marks a contrast with an outcome, not with the opening scene.

items.title: Ninety-Nine Times in a Hundred
items.theme: why an accurate screening test returns mostly false alarms when the condition it looks for is rare
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A cat-tier question-and-answer jumble whose tail is the contest. The illustration is written to be quotable so that it attracts the final seat, and the real closer is anchored to it by a figure the illustration alone produces. The imperative opening of the illustration also blocks it from the second seat.

items.title: One Voice From Each Side
items.theme: why a convention designed to keep reporters out of a dispute misreports the shape of the dispute, and the cheap repair
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A premium item built on one pronoun with two honest owners. Both candidate antecedents are plural, both are people, and the surrounding clause fits either reading; the tie is broken by a definite noun several words later. A heuristic solver following the nearest plural gets the second seat wrong and never recovers.

items.title: The Voice That Belongs to Neither
items.theme: the proposal that unmarked narration in a character's own idiom is what let the novel judge and sympathise at once
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A cat-tier hypothesis-support item whose trap is the macro pattern itself. Solvers taught that such paragraphs open on the hypothesis will place the second sentence first; the only evidence against them is a demonstrative. The specimen line is anchored in the final seat by a demonstrative of its own.

items.title: The Line Nature Does Not Draw
items.theme: why concepts without edges force institutions to supply boundaries that can be reasonable but never correct
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A medium item with two sentences that sound like verdicts. The separation is done by a definite description that repeats the content of the sentence it depends on, which is the cleanest kind of evidence a jumble can carry and worth drilling at this tier.

items.title: Having, and Being Allowed
items.theme: the replacement of ownership by revocable permission, and why the least glamorous cases are the ones that show it
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A premium five-sentence item whose whole difficulty is a false weld. Two parallel examples invite a solver to treat them as a unit, and the sentence that must sit between them is written to read perfectly well as a closing generalisation. The evidence against the weld is a superlative repeated across the two sentences it separates.

items.title: What a Price Can Take Away
items.theme: why paying people for something they were doing freely can reduce how much of it gets done
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A beginner item that introduces the definite article as a trap. Two sentences use the vocabulary of payment, and the definite noun phrase attaches to the later one; a single indefinite noun, a donation, is what proves it. Kept short and plain so the lesson is the reference, not the reading.

items.title: The Floor That Changed Places
items.theme: how the passenger lift turned the top of a building from the cheapest address into the dearest
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: An easy-tier chronology with one decoy opener. The lift sentence is the most interesting thing in the set and looks independent, and a single definite noun refuses it. A mild lexical decoy links the attic to the shed on the roof.

items.title: The Relatives Who Must Be Rude
items.theme: why compulsory mockery is licensed between exactly those kin whose cooperation is obligatory and whose interests collide
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A cat-tier claim-and-evidence item in which one word, insult, appears at the start and at the end and invites a weld. The evidence sentence has to sit between them, and the proof is a definite description in the closer that only the evidence can satisfy.

items.title: The Words Too Common to Tidy
items.theme: why the verbs that resist regular endings are almost always the ones speakers use every day
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: An easy item that teaches one high-value move: a presupposing noun beats a connective. Survivors cannot be counted until a loss has been reported, and that single word settles a seat that the But would otherwise win.

items.title: A Name for What They Were Doing
items.theme: why a word for the practitioner of science had to be coined, and what the coinage recorded about an older description
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A cat-tier question-and-answer item whose concrete sentence is deliberately the most attractive closer. Two definite nouns in the real closer take their referents from it, which is the evidence that settles the tail. The paired time adverbs fix the middle.

items.title: The Help That Nobody Claims
items.theme: why money offered to poor households goes uncollected, and why the cheapest reform is a shorter form
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A beginner problem-and-solution item built on one very reliable device: a counting phrase. The list has to precede the sentence that counts it, and the surface signals all agree with the meaning, so a careful reader solves it directly.

items.title: The One Who Did Nothing
items.theme: the proposal that our lighter judgement of omissions tracks the ease of identifying an agent rather than the gravity of the wrong
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A cat-plus item that sets two ordinals against each other. The scene offers a first and a second person; the question offers a first and a second explanation; and the sentence that says 'The second' names which kind it means only in the noun that follows it. Solvers who bind on the nearer pair lose the whole chain.

items.title: The Vote You Cannot Prove
items.theme: the secret ballot as a freedom protected by making evidence impossible rather than by forbidding pressure
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A ninety-nine tier five-sentence item in which two sentences are abstract maxims and either could open. The tie is broken by a clause at the end of one of them, which is the pattern this tier should drill. The tail is anchored by a counting phrase, so the contest is concentrated at the head.

items.title: Three Digits at a Time
items.theme: why grouping raises how much can be held in mind without the store itself growing
items.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md)
items.reviewer_notes: A beginner general-to-specific item. The example is written so that it borrows a phrase from the sentence before it, which is the cleanest way to teach that an illustration follows the claim it illustrates rather than the topic it shares words with.
